justification_text:
The point estimates at each horizon are driven by our best understanding of the likely trajectory of the target variable, factoring in both recent trends and longer-term expectations. For the 1-day forecast, the point estimate of 51.6 reflects a strong reliance on short-term momentum or near-term data, as this prediction is only looking ahead a very short time. By the 1-week horizon, the estimate shifts slightly to 51.8, indicating that while the trajectory doesn’t appear to be changing drastically, there is some room for modest adjustment as medium-term dynamics (such as smaller external influences or day-to-day variability) start to factor in. At the 1-month horizon, the point estimate rises further to 52.5. This reflects the idea that, over time, longer-term drivers (such as underlying trends, seasonality, or structural changes) have more time to take effect and may exert a more noticeable pull on the target variable, even if uncertainty is greater further out.

The confidence interval widths reflect layers of uncertainty that compound as the forecast horizon extends. For the 1-day forecast, the uncertainty is relatively narrow, spanning just 1.4 units (from 50.9 to 52.3). This reflects high confidence in the short term, as there is less time for unexpected events or random fluctuations to significantly alter the trajectory. By the 1-week horizon, the range widens considerably, reflecting greater potential for short-term shocks, variability in inputs, or compounding errors from short-term assumptions. At the 1-month horizon, the confidence interval is particularly wide, from 48.5 to 56.5, illustrating the sheer difficulty of accurately forecasting outcomes over longer timeframes. Over such periods, there is much greater uncertainty around external factors, trend shifts, or random noise.

Certain risks or events could push outcomes outside the stated confidence intervals. In the short term (1-day or 1-week), abrupt shocks such as unexpected news, policy decisions, or market anomalies could influence outcomes. Over a longer timeframe (1 month), there is greater exposure to structural shifts, such as changes in economic conditions, geopolitical events, or the emergence of new information that fundamentally alters the context. Even rare or extreme tail events, though unlikely, cannot be ruled out entirely. While the confidence intervals attempt to account for many plausible scenarios, extreme moves—particularly those tied to unpredictable events—could fall outside the predicted ranges.
